newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan refugees told to leave Tanzania this month.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan refugees told to leave Tanzania this month.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency and Tanzanian government told more than half a million Rwandan refugees in Tanzania on Thursday to go home by the end of this month.

"The government of Tanzania has set a target date of 31 December 1996, by which time all Rwandan refugees in Tanzania are expected to have returned home," said a statement from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to the refugees.

"The Tanzanian government has assured UNHCR of its commitment that the repatriation process will be carried out in an orderly and humane manner," it said. "UNHCR therefore urges that all refugees make preparations to return before that date."
It said Tanzania had concluded all Rwandan refugees could return safely home following the return to Rwanda of 600,000 refugees from Zaire and 80,000 refugees from Burundi.

While UNHCR officials emphasised repatriation was voluntary, it was unclear what would happen to those who refuse. A UNHCR official, who declined to be named, said it was possible that after the December 31 deadline Rwandans who refused to return home could lose refugee status.
Refugees, such as the elderly, infirm, disabled, pregnant or unnacompanied minors, should register with UNHCR by December 9 to arrange assistance to return home, the UNHCR statement said.
A total of 542,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fled to eastern Tanzania in 1994 during civil war and genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
UNHCR and Tanzanian officials have sought a mass return from Tanzania since the estimated 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees trekked home from east Zaire camps between November 15 and 19.
Some aid workers have warned triggering an exodus from Tanzania will be difficult and note refugees left eastern Zaire only because fighting forced them from their camps near the Rwandan border.
Many refugees in Tanzania, like those who were in Zaire, said they feared going home because they might be jailed or attacked in reprisal for the genocide, which some took part in.
Aid workers say Hutu extremist militiamen and former Rwandan troops who have ordered refugees not to return must be separated before large numbers of innocent refugees can be expected to go.

"If people are refusing to go back when perhaps one million will have returned by the 31st, there would be strong reasons to believe they would not be bona fide refugees and could have taken part in the events of 1994 (genocide)," said the official.
UNHCR sources told Reuters the Tanzanian government had a list of 200 intimidators who might be separated from the main body of refugees prior to the repatriation deadline.

Lennart Kotsalainen, deputy head of the office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Tanzania's capital, said radio broadcasts were being made to inform the refugees of the departure order.
"Obviously some will be very hesitant but once the ball starts rolling probably it will be a mass return," Kotsalainen said.
UNHCR said the Home Affairs (Interior) Ministry would be responsible for the repatriation and police would protect refugees and would be supported, if necessary, by troops.
